preface: This volume follows a change in the balance of the war that was easier to recognize afterwards than to direct at the time. In January 1943, Soviet armies were advancing while the fighting at Stalingrad continued. By July 1944, they had driven the German front far to the west and destroyed much of Army Group Centre. Between those points lay costly reverses, incomplete victories, and repeated efforts to turn battlefield success into an advance that could be sustained.

I have tried to follow that development without allowing the outcome to settle every earlier question. The German counterstroke at Kharkov was a serious Soviet defeat. The failure of Citadel did not make every subsequent Soviet attack successful. Bagration emerged from preparations and decisions whose effectiveness must be explained, rather than assumed from the scale of the victory. Commanders acted on reports that were incomplete or already out of date, with formations whose strength could change sharply between an order and its execution.

The account begins by returning to January 1943. That overlap with the struggle at Stalingrad is deliberate. The German withdrawal from the Caucasus and the Soviet advances towards Kharkov were already under way before the pocket had been eliminated. Following them from their beginnings makes it possible to see how the winter victories created opportunities that the Red Army could not yet exploit consistently, and how the resulting reverses shaped the preparations for Kursk.

From there, the volume follows the summer offensives, the advance to the Dnieper, and the fighting that carried Soviet armies beyond it. The campaigns of 1944 begin in the north with the relief of Leningrad, then return to Ukraine and Crimea before turning to Finland and Belarus. These movements overlapped. I have kept related operations together so that their purposes and consequences remain clear, returning to the wider front where changes elsewhere affected the forces available.

As in the earlier volumes, military operations are inseparable from the people living through them. German retreat brought deliberate destruction, forced removals, and further murders. The end of German occupation enabled survivors to emerge from hiding and allowed recovery to begin, but it could not restore the communities already destroyed. The return of Soviet authority brought its own demands and coercion. In Crimea, the deportation of the Crimean Tatars followed a separate decision by Stalin and the security authorities; it was not an inevitable consequence of the military victory.

The narrative closes during July 1944, after the loss of Minsk, Vilnius, and Grodno had transformed Germany’s central position. This is a boundary within the summer campaign, not the end of Bagration in its full operational sense. German resistance was beginning to regain coherence farther west, while the Soviet advance was opening further military opportunities and disputes over political authority. Those developments belong to the continuation of the history.

My purpose remains to explain what an operation achieved, what it failed to decide, and what was required to carry its results forward. The scale of this war can make armies and populations appear as totals. Following the roads, decisions, institutions, and individual experiences behind those totals helps recover something of the circumstances in which people fought and survived. Thank you for continuing that history with me.
noteToReader: This volume covers the Eastern Front from January 1943 through July 1944. Its six parts retain the series numbering, XIII–XVIII, within Sections V and VI. Chapters are numbered consecutively from 1 to 35 within the volume. Section V follows the struggle for the initiative during 1943; Section VI follows the northern, southern, and central campaigns of 1944 to the volume’s July endpoint.

The chapters follow connected campaigns rather than moving every theatre forward in strict daily sequence. The opening returns to the weeks before the fighting at Stalingrad ended. Later parts likewise return to the beginning of operations already under way elsewhere. Chapter dates provide orientation: an account may refer back to preparations or briefly follow consequences beyond its stated period when the subject requires it.

The final part covers the preparation and opening destruction of Bagration and the pursuit towards Vilnius and Grodno. It also follows the overlapping offensive against Finland. The summer campaign continued beyond July; later operations and political settlements are not treated here as completed outcomes.

Place names generally follow the period and the sources used, with modern equivalents supplied where they help identify a location. Military designations identify formations and commands, not the nationality of every person serving in them. Figures for casualties, prisoners, and equipment losses are qualified where their definitions or coverage differ. A damaged tank, a permanent vehicle loss, and a vehicle temporarily unavailable for service are not interchangeable categories.

Supporting references appear in the Notes at the end of the volume. They are numbered continuously and link to the consolidated Bibliography, which identifies editions, translations, and published or online reproductions. Qualifications about the material consulted remain with the relevant entries and notes. The narrative can be read independently of the website.

5: The destruction of Sixth Army at Stalingrad left other German armies in the field and the Soviet formations pursuing them depleted. Fuel, ammunition, and replacements had to cross the distances opened by the leading tanks. Further advance depended on restoring the strength needed to sustain it.

During 1943, the struggle for the initiative increasingly concerned the ability to renew operations. German commanders could still concentrate powerful forces and inflict serious defeats. Their difficulty was to make those successes produce a strategic result Germany could sustain. Soviet commanders had growing resources, but had to employ them without repeatedly exposing their mobile formations to destruction.

The campaigns also changed the conditions of occupation. German withdrawals brought destruction and forced removals. Partisan forces expanded, Jewish resistance confronted extermination, and civilians faced armed movements with incompatible political purposes. Military liberation and political freedom could not be treated as interchangeable achievements.

The account returns to January 1943, while fighting at Stalingrad continued, to follow the Caucasus withdrawal and Soviet offensives farther north. Their opportunities and failures shaped the summer preparations without determining the outcome.
6: By early 1944, the Red Army could compel the German command to answer major offensives in widely separated theatres. German counterattacks could still defeat an advancing Soviet formation, but transferring reserves to one emergency increased the danger elsewhere. Germany held extensive territory with fewer means of choosing where the next sustained battle would occur.

Soviet commanders still had to concentrate supplies, identify usable breakthroughs, and bring supporting forces forward. Methods that worked outside Leningrad required adjustment at a river in Estonia or a junction in Ukraine. Successive victories could contribute to the same strategic advance while arising from different operational circumstances.

The account begins with Leningrad’s relief and the advance towards Estonia and Pskov. It then returns to the overlapping campaigns in Ukraine and Crimea before following the summer offensive in Belarus. Each advance depended on the condition of the formations that reached the next German position.

Soviet authorities restored services and demanded labour and recruits. Beyond the prewar Soviet borders, their advance also raised questions of sovereignty and competing claims to political authority.

13: Across the southern front, the winter advance carried Soviet forces towards railway junctions and river crossings whose loss threatened much larger German groupings. Rostov controlled the most useful land exit from the Caucasus. Kharkov connected routes across eastern Ukraine. Beyond it, the Donbas and the approaches to the Dnieper offered opportunities to sever the communications of the armies retreating from the Don. These were related objectives, but they demanded different forces and could not all be secured simply by continuing the pursuit.

The winter campaigns joined successive Soviet advances to a German counteroffensive against exposed mobile formations. In the centre, the evacuation of the Rzhev salient released German forces by shortening the front. Behind the armies, resistance and repression followed their own geography and political pressures. Those struggles extend into the summer in this part, before the account returns to the military preparations of April–June.
14: The German offensive that opened on July 5 was intended to destroy the Soviet armies in the Kursk salient and restore Germany’s freedom of action in the east. Its failure emerged through separate battles on the northern and southern faces, where prepared positions, mobile reserves, artillery, and infantry resisted attacks of unequal strength. Neither a breached trench line nor the outcome of a single tank engagement could settle the larger contest.

While those battles continued, the Soviet command brought other operations into motion. The attack against Orel began before Citadel had ended; attacks on the Donets and Mius followed in July; the offensive against Belgorod and Kharkov opened in August. These operations did not advance at the same speed or achieve everything intended. Together they made it increasingly difficult for German commanders to assemble the reserves needed to recover from one crisis before another developed.

Soviet forces continued attacking despite costly defensive battles and local defeats. Formations repeatedly had to be rebuilt, while civilians endured renewed fighting and forced removal from the territory through which the armies moved. Sustaining the offensive required resources and recovery as well as the success of the first attack.
15: The Soviet victories of the summer opened the way to a wider advance, but the German retreat did not settle the campaign. Between August and December 1943, the fighting spread from Smolensk and Nevel to the Donbas, the Dnieper crossings, and the approaches west of Kiev. Soviet commanders had to turn pursuit into sustained operations across major rivers. German commanders sought to preserve their armies, establish a defensible front, and strike at advances which had become exposed.

The recovery of territory also ended occupation in devastated communities. Demolition, forced evacuation, mass murder, and the concealment of crimes accompanied the German withdrawal. Returning Soviet authority brought reconstruction and renewed demands upon survivors. The advance to the Dnieper therefore joined the contest between armies to the fate of the people living on the ground they fought over. By the end of the year, the Soviet Union held the strategic initiative and major positions beyond the river, while the next offensive was already beginning.
16: The northern campaign opened against a front that had remained comparatively stable while the war moved across enormous distances farther south. Leningrad was still threatened by German artillery. Its land connection, opened in January 1943, had improved supply without removing the enemy from the city’s approaches. Along the Volkhov and around Lake Ilmen, fortified positions continued to separate armies that had fought over the same difficult country for years.

In January 1944, Soviet attacks from the Oranienbaum bridgehead, the southern outskirts of Leningrad and the Novgorod sector began to pull that defensive system apart. Their immediate purpose was the city’s complete relief; their developing opportunity was the defeat of the German Eighteenth Army. The two objectives were connected, although the first could be achieved before the second. The German retreat carried the battle westwards, across the Luga and towards a shorter defensive position on the Narva River and the approaches to Pskov.

The northern campaign ended the siege without completing Leningrad’s recovery or destroying Army Group North. By spring, Soviet forces had reached Estonia and the approaches to Pskov, where further advances met sustained resistance. The five chapters in this part follow both the fighting and the difficult beginnings of civilian recovery behind the new front.
17: The southern campaign of 1944 grew out of positions won during the preceding autumn. Soviet armies already stood west of the Dnieper, but German forces still held much of Ukraine, retained a bridgehead across the lower river, and occupied Crimea. Their defeat required several connected offensives. These operations overlapped in time without producing identical results: a pocket could be closed yet fail to yield the destruction of the army within it, while the loss of a railway junction could force a withdrawal far beyond the battlefield on which it had been captured.

The advance carried the Red Army from the approaches to Kiev towards the Carpathians, the Dniester and Romania. It ended German and Romanian occupation across a large region, exposed the evidence of mass murder, and restored Soviet institutions. In Crimea, the recovery of the peninsula was followed by the deportation of the Crimean Tatars. Military victory and the exercise of state power must therefore be followed together, with the decisions and responsibilities of each institution kept clear. We return first to late December 1943, when the struggle west of Kiev opened the next stage of the southern war.
18: The German armies still holding Belarus in the spring of 1944 occupied a position which Soviet forces had repeatedly failed to break. Their survival was no guarantee that the position could withstand a differently prepared attack. During the next months, Soviet headquarters assembled the means to strike several sectors together, penetrate beyond the forward defences and prevent the surviving German formations from assembling farther west. The destruction of Army Group Centre emerged from that sequence of decisions and operations.

The summer campaign also opened against Finland, whose army, government and political purposes require a separate account. In Belarus, victory carried Soviet forces into devastated communities and towards territories whose future government was disputed. The following chapters move from preparation to the successive encirclements, then follow the pursuit to Vilnius and Grodno. They end with the German front being reconstructed farther west and the conflict over political authority becoming inseparable from the military advance.
